The [[governor of Michigan]] is the [[head of government]] of the [[U.S. state]] of [[Michigan]]. In 1805, the [[Michigan Territory]] was created, and five men served as territorial governors, until Michigan was granted statehood in 1837. Forty-seven individuals have held the position of state governor. The first female governor, [[Jennifer Granholm]], served from 2003 to 2011. The longest-serving governor in Michigan's history was [[William Milliken]], who was promoted from lieutenant governor after Governor [[George W. Romney]] resigned to become [[United States Secretary of Housing and Urban Development|Secretary of Housing and Urban Development]], then was elected to three further successive terms. The only governors to serve non-consecutive terms were [[John S. Barry]] and [[Frank Fitzgerald]].

==List of governors==

===Territory of Michigan===

[[Michigan Territory]] was organized on June 30, 1805, from the north half of [[Indiana Territory]].<ref>{{usstat|2|309}}</ref> It had three governors appointed by the [[president of the United States]], including the longest-serving governor of any territory, [[Lewis Cass]], who served for 18 years. During the [[War of 1812]], following the [[Siege of Detroit]] and [[British occupation of the Michigan Territory|British occupation of Michigan Territory]], Colonel [[Henry Procter (British Army officer)|Henry Procter]] was appointed as civil governor.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hitsman |first1=J. Mackay |last2=Graves |first2=Donald E. |title=The Incredible War of 1812 |publisher=Robin Brass Studio |year=1999 |isbn=978-1896941134 |url=https://archive.org/details/incrediblewarof10000hits_p0g9 |url-access=registration |pages=85–88 |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/capture-of-detroit-war-of-1812 |last=Marsh |first=James H. |date=March 4, 2015 |access-date=October 30, 2026 |title=Capture of Detroit, War of 1812 |website=[[The Canadian Encyclopedia]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200323031541/https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/capture-of-detroit-war-of-1812 |archive-date=March 23, 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref>

===State of Michigan===
Michigan was [[Admission to the Union|admitted to the Union]] on January 26, 1837. Under the original [[constitution of Michigan]], governors held the office for a two-year term,{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1935|loc=1835 art. V, § 1}}, until the 1963 [[Constitution of Michigan|Michigan Constitution]] changed the term to four years.{{sfn|Mich. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/mi/constitution/section-id-79162 1963 art. V, 21]}} There was no [[term limit]] until a 1992 constitutional amendment imposed a lifetime limit of two terms.{{sfn|Mich. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/mi/constitution/section-id-79192 1992 art. V, § 30]}} 

Should the office of governor become vacant, the [[Lieutenant Governor of Michigan|lieutenant governor]] becomes governor, followed in order of succession by the [[Michigan Secretary of State|secretary of state]] and the [[Michigan Attorney General|attorney general]].{{sfn|Mich. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/mi/constitution/section-id-79180 1963 art. V, § 26]}} Prior to the current constitution, the duties of the office would devolve upon the lieutenant governor, without that person actually becoming governor.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1936|loc=1835 art. V, § 12}} Since 1850, the term begins at noon on the January 1 following the election;{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1957|loc=1850 art. VIII, § 2}} before, it had no set start date, and terms would last until when their successor was inaugurated, which would be at least the first Monday in January following their election.{{sfn|Thorpe|1909|p=1940|loc=1835 art. XII, § 10}} Since 1963, the governor and lieutenant governor have been elected on the same [[Ticket (election)|ticket]].{{sfn|Mich. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/mi/constitution/section-id-79162 1963 art. V, 21]}}
